concepts.tip: AIC = CIA reversed. Remember: CIA triad, same three goals.
concepts.def: Core security model: Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality — the three goals every security program must protect.
concepts.ex: A firewall protects confidentiality; checksums protect integrity; clustering ensures availability.

concepts.tip: Availability = Always accessible. Downtime is an availability failure.
concepts.def: Ensures systems and data are accessible to authorized users when needed.
concepts.ex: 99.9% uptime SLA; redundant power supplies; load balancing.

concepts.tip: Integrity = Identical to original. No tampering.
concepts.def: Ensures data is accurate, complete, and has not been improperly modified.
concepts.ex: Hash verification of downloaded files; digital signatures on emails.

concepts.tip: Confidentiality = secret. Only cleared eyes see it.
concepts.def: Ensures information is accessible only to those who are authorized to see it.
concepts.ex: AES encryption of stored files; TLS for data in transit.

concepts.tip: Preventive = before. Stops the threat at the gate.
concepts.def: Controls that stop security incidents before they occur.
concepts.ex: Firewalls, access control lists, security awareness training.

concepts.tip: Detective = discover. Finds what happened after the fact.
concepts.def: Controls that identify and record security incidents after they occur.
concepts.ex: IDS alerts, audit logs, CCTV cameras.

concepts.tip: Corrective = cure. Fixes the damage after detection.
concepts.def: Controls that reduce the impact of an incident and restore systems to normal.
concepts.ex: Patching exploited software, restoring from backup, quarantining malware.

concepts.tip: Deterrent = discourage. Makes attackers think twice.
concepts.def: Controls that discourage attackers from attempting a security violation.
concepts.ex: Warning banners, visible cameras, security guards.

concepts.tip: Recovery = rebuild. Gets you back to normal operations.
concepts.def: Controls that restore capabilities after a security incident or disaster.
concepts.ex: Disaster recovery plan, backup restoration, failover site.

concepts.tip: Administrative = paperwork controls. Policies and procedures.
concepts.def: Policies, procedures, and guidelines governing security behavior and management decisions.
concepts.ex: Acceptable use policy, security training program, hiring background checks.

concepts.tip: Physical = you can touch it. Fences, locks, cameras.
concepts.def: Tangible measures protecting facilities, hardware, and personnel from physical threats.
concepts.ex: Locks, fences, guards, CCTV cameras, fire suppression.

concepts.tip: Technical = tech controls. Software and hardware safeguards.
concepts.def: Logical controls implemented via hardware or software to protect systems and data.
concepts.ex: Encryption, firewalls, antivirus, access control lists.

concepts.tip: Security Program = the master plan. Strategy before tools.
concepts.def: Process of building an organization's overall security strategy, policies, and control framework.
concepts.ex: CISO develops information security policy aligned with ISO 27001 and NIST CSF.

concepts.tip: 27000 = ISMS standards. 27001 certify, 27002 guide.
concepts.def: International family of standards defining requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS).
concepts.ex: ISO 27001 certifies ISMS; ISO 27002 provides control guidance.

concepts.tip: EA = blueprint of the entire organization's IT.
concepts.def: Holistic approach aligning an organization's IT infrastructure with its business strategy and goals.
concepts.ex: Using TOGAF ADM to map current and target-state architecture.

concepts.tip: Zachman = grid. Rows × Columns = perspectives × questions.
concepts.def: 2D matrix organizing enterprise architecture by stakeholder perspective (rows) and interrogative concern (columns).
concepts.ex: Rows: owner, designer, builder; columns: what, how, where, who, when, why.

concepts.tip: TOGAF = The Open Group = ADM cycle for EA.
concepts.def: The Open Group Architecture Framework — structured EA method using the Architecture Development Method (ADM).
concepts.ex: ADM phases guide architecture from vision through implementation and governance.

concepts.tip: DoDAF/MODAF = military EA. Defense-focused blueprints.
concepts.def: Architectures (DoDAF, MODAF) designed for defense and military systems planning and interoperability.
concepts.ex: DoDAF viewpoints: operational, systems, services, technical.

concepts.tip: MODAF = UK military version of DoDAF.
concepts.def: UK Ministry of Defence Architecture Framework for planning and communicating military systems.
concepts.ex: Used to model joint military operations and equipment interoperability.

concepts.def: U.S. Department of Defense architecture framework that ensures interoperability of systems to meet military mission goals
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Enterprise Architecture Development › Military-Oriented Architecture Frameworks
ESA = security baked into EA, not bolted on.
concepts.def: Integrates security requirements and controls into every layer of enterprise architecture.
concepts.ex: SABSA framework mapping business risks to security services.

concepts.def: provides a life-cycle model so that the architecture can be constantly monitored and improved upon over time.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Enterprise Architecture Development › Enterprise Security Architecture
Controls development = pick and build the right safeguards.
concepts.def: Process of selecting and implementing safeguards based on risk assessment and compliance requirements.
concepts.ex: Mapping NIST SP 800-53 controls to identified risks.

concepts.tip: COBIT = IT governance. Business goals ↔ IT controls.
concepts.def: Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies — IT governance and management framework.
concepts.ex: Five principles: meeting stakeholder needs, covering enterprise end-to-end, single framework.

concepts.tip: 800-53 = the US federal control catalog. AC, AU, SI families.
concepts.def: US federal catalog of security and privacy controls for information systems and organizations.
concepts.ex: AC-2 (account management), AU-6 (audit review), SI-3 (malicious code protection).

concepts.tip: COSO = 5 components for internal control. SOX compliance.
concepts.def: Framework providing guidance on internal controls with five interrelated components.
concepts.ex: Used by public companies to demonstrate SOX compliance.

concepts.tip: COSO 17 principles = one set per each of the 5 components.
concepts.def: COSO's detailed principles covering governance, risk assessment, control activities, information, and monitoring.
concepts.ex: Principle 1: Demonstrates commitment to integrity and ethical values.

concepts.tip: Control Environment = culture and tone. Foundation of COSO.
concepts.def: COSO component establishing the tone at the top — ethics, oversight, and organizational structure.
concepts.ex: Board audit committee, code of conduct, HR policies.

concepts.tip: Risk Assessment = find and analyze threats to objectives.
concepts.def: COSO component for identifying and analyzing risks that could prevent achieving objectives.
concepts.ex: Fraud risk assessment; IT risk register; threat modeling.

concepts.tip: Control Activities = the actual controls doing the work.
concepts.def: COSO component — policies and procedures ensuring management directives are executed.
concepts.ex: Approval workflows, reconciliations, access controls, physical controls.

concepts.tip: Info & Comm = right info to right people at right time.
concepts.def: COSO component — relevant information must be identified, captured, and communicated timely.
concepts.ex: Security dashboards, incident reporting channels, whistleblower hotlines.

concepts.tip: Monitoring = check that controls keep working over time.
concepts.def: COSO component — ongoing and periodic evaluations verifying internal controls are present and working.
concepts.ex: Continuous monitoring tools, internal audit reviews, management self-assessments.

concepts.tip: Process mgmt = how to improve how you do things.
concepts.def: Frameworks for improving and maturing organizational processes systematically.
concepts.ex: CMMI guiding software development process improvement.

concepts.tip: ITIL = IT service management best practices. Five life-cycle stages.
concepts.def: IT Infrastructure Library — best-practice framework for IT service management lifecycle.
concepts.ex: ITIL incident management, change management, service desk practices.

concepts.def: Its goal is to improve process quality by using statistical methods of measuring operation efficiency and reducing variation, defects, and waste
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Process Management Development
CMMI = 5 levels: Initial → Managed → Defined → Quantitative → Optimizing.
concepts.def: Process improvement framework with five maturity levels guiding organizations from chaotic to optimized.
concepts.ex: CMMI Level 3 means all processes are documented and standardized.

concepts.tip: CMMI levels 1–5: think of climbing stairs toward optimization.
concepts.def: CMMI has five maturity levels (1–5) measuring process capability and discipline.
concepts.ex: Level 1: chaotic. Level 3: defined. Level 5: optimizing.

concepts.tip: Level 0 = chaos before Level 1. Not formally in CMMI.
concepts.def: Informal concept below CMMI Level 1 representing no recognizable process in place.
concepts.ex: No documentation, no repeatability — pure firefighting mode.

concepts.tip: Nonexistent = random results. No process, no predictability.
concepts.def: State below CMMI Level 1 where no management process exists; outcomes are entirely unpredictable.
concepts.ex: Projects succeed or fail based solely on individual heroics.

concepts.tip: Level 1 = heroic individuals. Unpredictable, no discipline.
concepts.def: CMMI Initial level — processes are ad hoc and chaotic; success depends on individual effort.
concepts.ex: Each developer follows their own process; no shared standards.

concepts.tip: Unpredictable = Level 1 chaos. Same input, different output.
concepts.def: CMMI Level 1 characteristic: no stable, repeatable process exists; results vary widely.
concepts.ex: Two projects of identical size deliver wildly different quality and schedules.

concepts.tip: Repeatable = Level 2. Can do it again if same type of project.
concepts.def: CMMI Level 2 — basic project management established; similar projects can be repeated successfully.
concepts.ex: Requirements management and project planning processes in place.

concepts.tip: Defined = Level 3. One standard process for everyone.
concepts.def: CMMI Level 3 — processes documented, standardized, and proactively managed org-wide.
concepts.ex: Standard software development process used across all projects.

concepts.tip: Level 4 = metrics drive decisions. Data-controlled processes.
concepts.def: CMMI Quantitatively Managed level — processes measured and controlled using quantitative data.
concepts.ex: Statistical process control applied to defect rates and cycle time.

concepts.tip: Managed = measured. Numbers tell you if the process is in control.
concepts.def: CMMI Level 4 characteristic: statistical process control applied to manage performance.
concepts.ex: Control charts tracking defect injection rates across sprints.

concepts.tip: Level 5 = always improving. Never stop getting better.
concepts.def: CMMI Optimizing level — continuous improvement driven by quantitative feedback and innovation.
concepts.ex: Root cause analysis used to prevent defect categories permanently.

concepts.tip: Optimized = Level 5 pinnacle. Improvement is the process.
concepts.def: CMMI Level 5 characteristic: focus on continuous process improvement and defect prevention.
concepts.ex: Lessons learned systematically fed back to improve the standard process.

concepts.def: Management’s support is one of the most important pieces of a security program

Life cycle = birth to death. Every system has one.
concepts.def: Structured set of phases from initiation through disposal governing systems or projects.
concepts.ex: SDLC phases: planning, analysis, design, implementation, maintenance, disposal.

concepts.cat: The Crux of Computer Crime Laws
concepts.tip: 1029 = access device fraud. Cards, PINs, counterfeit devices.
concepts.def: US federal law targeting fraud and related activity in connection with access devices (credit cards, PINs).
concepts.ex: Counterfeiting credit cards or selling stolen card numbers violates 18 USC 1029.

concepts.cat: The Crux of Computer Crime Laws
concepts.tip: 1030 = CFAA. Unauthorized computer access is a federal crime.
concepts.def: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act — prohibits unauthorized access to protected computer systems.
concepts.ex: Hacking a government database or installing malware violates 18 USC 1030.

concepts.tip: Common schemes = phishing, BEC, ransomware. Report to IC3.
concepts.def: FBI-identified online fraud schemes including phishing, BEC, ransomware, and romance scams.
concepts.ex: IC3 reports billions lost annually to BEC and investment fraud.

concepts.tip: International = jurisdiction gap. Laws don't cross borders easily.
concepts.def: Differences in jurisdiction and laws across countries complicate cross-border cybercrime prosecution.
concepts.ex: Attacker in country A attacks victim in country B — whose law applies?

concepts.tip: GDPR = EU privacy law. 72-hour breach notice, huge fines.
concepts.def: EU regulation protecting personal data and privacy rights of EU residents, effective May 2018.
concepts.ex: GDPR requires breach notification within 72 hours and imposes fines up to 4% of global revenue.

concepts.tip: Data subject = the person the data is ABOUT.
concepts.def: The natural person whose personal data is collected, processed, or stored.
concepts.ex: A customer whose name and email are in a company database is a data subject.

concepts.tip: Controller = decides WHY and HOW data is processed.
concepts.def: Entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.
concepts.ex: A hospital deciding to collect patient records is the data controller.

concepts.tip: Processor = does the work FOR the controller.
concepts.def: Entity that processes personal data on behalf of and under instructions from the data controller.
concepts.ex: A cloud payroll vendor processing employee data for an employer.

concepts.tip: Role = who controls vs. who processes. Different GDPR duties.
concepts.def: GDPR distinguishes controller vs. processor roles to assign accountability for data protection.
concepts.ex: SaaS vendor is processor; the business using the SaaS is the controller.

concepts.tip: DPO = GDPR compliance watchdog. Mandatory in many cases.
concepts.def: GDPR-mandated officer ensuring organizational compliance with data protection law.
concepts.ex: DPO required for public authorities and large-scale processing of sensitive data.

concepts.tip: GDPR key = lawful basis + rights + DPO + 72h breach + 4% fine.
concepts.def: Lawful basis, data subject rights, DPO requirement, breach notification, and fines up to 4% of revenue.
concepts.ex: Organizations must identify a lawful basis (consent, contract, legitimate interest) for every processing activity.

concepts.tip: Consent = freely given + specific + informed + unambiguous.
concepts.def: Freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous agreement to personal data processing.
concepts.ex: Pre-ticked opt-in boxes do not constitute valid GDPR consent.

concepts.def: Data controllers and data processors must inform data subjects about how their data is, will, or could be used.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 2016 › Key provisions of the GDPR
Restrict = pause processing while dispute is resolved.
concepts.def: Data subject can limit how their data is used while a dispute or complaint is being resolved.
concepts.ex: User contests data accuracy — controller must restrict processing pending verification.

concepts.tip: Right to be forgotten = erasure request right under GDPR.
concepts.def: Right to erasure — individuals can request deletion of their personal data under certain conditions.
concepts.ex: Former employee requests deletion of their data after contract ends.

concepts.tip: Breach = notify authority in 72h, individuals if high risk.
concepts.def: Security incidents leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, or disclosure of personal data.
concepts.ex: Database exposed online — GDPR requires notifying supervisory authority within 72 hours.

concepts.tip: Import/export = data can't flow freely across all borders.
concepts.def: Laws restricting cross-border transfer of personal data and export of cryptographic products.
concepts.ex: GDPR restricts transferring EU personal data to countries without adequate protection.

concepts.tip: Legal systems = civil, common, religious, customary. Jurisdiction matters.
concepts.def: Civil law, common law, religious law, and customary law — each handles cybercrime prosecution differently.
concepts.ex: US uses common law; France uses civil law — different evidentiary standards.

concepts.def: Civil law generally is derived from common law (case law)

concepts.def: Non-criminal legal action seeking financial damages for harm caused by negligence or wrongdoing.

Piracy = copying software without paying. Copyright infringement.
concepts.def: Unauthorized copying, distribution, or use of copyrighted software without a valid license.
concepts.ex: Installing one licensed copy of software on 50 machines.

concepts.tip: DMCA = no DRM cracking. Safe harbor for ISPs.
concepts.def: US law criminalizing circumvention of copyright protection measures and ISP safe harbors.
concepts.ex: Breaking DRM on a DVD violates the DMCA anti-circumvention provision.

concepts.tip: Copyright Directive = EU's DMCA equivalent for the digital age.
concepts.def: EU directive aligning copyright law with the digital environment, including upload filters and press publisher rights.
concepts.ex: Article 17 requires platforms to prevent upload of copyrighted content.

concepts.tip: PII = anything that identifies YOU as a specific person.
concepts.def: Any data that can identify a specific individual directly or in combination with other data.
concepts.ex: Name, SSN, email, biometrics, IP address, passport number.

concepts.tip: PII components: name + contact + ID numbers + biometrics.
concepts.def: PII components include name, address, SSN, date of birth, email, phone, and biometric data.
concepts.ex: Health record combining name + DOB + diagnosis constitutes sensitive PII.

concepts.tip: Privacy law = controls what orgs can do with your personal data.
concepts.def: Privacy laws regulate the collection, storage, use, and disclosure of personal information.
concepts.ex: GDPR (EU), CCPA (California), HIPAA (US health) — each with different requirements.

concepts.def: US federal law protecting the privacy and security of health information (PHI).
concepts.ex: Hospital must encrypt patient records and train staff on PHI handling.

Levels = sensitivity hierarchy. Higher level = more protection.
concepts.def: Hierarchical tiers assigning sensitivity to data — e.g., Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Unclassified.
concepts.ex: Military: TS/SCI > Secret > Confidential. Commercial: Restricted > Internal > Public.

concepts.tip: Controls follow classification. Higher class = stronger controls.
concepts.def: Safeguards applied based on data classification: encryption, access restrictions, handling procedures.
concepts.ex: Top Secret data requires two-person integrity and encrypted storage.

concepts.tip: Procedures = classify at birth, review regularly, declassify when safe.
concepts.def: Steps to assign, review, downgrade, and declassify information throughout its lifecycle.
concepts.ex: Owner classifies on creation; periodic reviews determine if downgrade is appropriate.

concepts.tip: Exec Mgmt = tone at the top. They own ultimate accountability.
concepts.def: C-suite sets security culture, risk appetite, and provides resources for the security program.
concepts.ex: CEO signs the information security policy; CFO approves the security budget.

concepts.tip: CEO = ultimate accountability. The buck stops here.
concepts.def: Ultimately accountable for organizational risk and security posture at the board level.
concepts.ex: CEO held liable after major breach due to inadequate security investment.

concepts.tip: Data Owner = business person who decides classification and controls.
concepts.def: Business manager responsible for data classification and determining protection requirements.
concepts.ex: HR director is data owner for employee records — sets retention and access rules.

concepts.def: is responsible for maintaining and protecting the data.

System Owner = IT person who implements what data owner requires.
concepts.def: IT manager responsible for the system that processes or stores data.
concepts.ex: Database administrator owns the HR system and implements the controls data owner requires.

concepts.def: is responsible for implementing and maintaining specific security network devices and software in the enterprise

Retention policy = what to keep, how long, then destroy.
concepts.def: Defining what data to keep, how long to keep it, in what format, and when to destroy it.
concepts.ex: Legal holds financial records for 7 years; marketing data deleted after 2 years.

concepts.tip: How to retain = medium + location + protection method.
concepts.def: Deciding on storage media, location, encryption, and access controls for retained data.
concepts.ex: Encrypted tape backup stored off-site in fireproof vault with restricted access.

concepts.def: A taxonomy is a scheme for classifying data. This classification can be made using a variety of categories,
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · How We Retain
What to retain = driven by law, regulation, and litigation need.
concepts.def: Determined by legal, regulatory, business, and litigation hold requirements.
concepts.ex: HIPAA requires 6-year retention of medical records; SOX requires 7 years for financials.

concepts.tip: EDRM = e-discovery roadmap. 9 stages from data to court.
concepts.def: Framework for e-discovery covering information governance through production and presentation.
concepts.ex: EDRM stages: identification → preservation → collection → processing → review → production.

concepts.tip: Remanence = ghost of deleted data. Lingers on media.
concepts.def: Residual representation of data remaining on storage media after deletion or reformatting.
concepts.ex: Deleted file still recoverable with forensic tools because sectors not overwritten.

concepts.tip: Erasing = only removes pointer. Data still there.
concepts.def: Removing a file's directory entry; data remains physically present and is easily recoverable.
concepts.ex: Pressing Delete in Windows — file appears gone but data still on disk.

concepts.tip: Clearing = write over data. Stops casual recovery.
concepts.def: Writing new data patterns over storage to prevent casual recovery of sensitive data.
concepts.ex: DoD 5220.22-M overwrite standard — 3-pass overwrite of disk sectors.

concepts.tip: Purging = thorough. Lab-proof data removal.
concepts.def: More thorough than clearing — removes data so it cannot be recovered even by lab techniques.
concepts.ex: Cryptographic erasure of encryption keys making data permanently inaccessible.

concepts.tip: Degaussing = magnetic wipe. Only for magnetic media.
concepts.def: Using a powerful magnetic field to destroy data stored on magnetic media.
concepts.ex: Degaussing hard drives and backup tapes before disposal.

concepts.tip: Sanitization = make media safe. Clear, purge, or destroy.
concepts.def: Process of rendering data inaccessible on media to make it safe for reuse, donation, or disposal.
concepts.ex: NIST SP 800-88 guidelines: clear for reuse, purge for recycling, destroy for disposal.

concepts.tip: Data security controls = the full protection toolkit for data.
concepts.def: Technical and administrative measures protecting data confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
concepts.ex: Encryption, access controls, DLP, data classification, and backup.

concepts.def: The solution to protecting data in such scenarios is as simple as it is ubiquitous: encryption.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Data Security Controls
Data in motion = on the wire. Protect with TLS or VPN.
concepts.def: Data actively being transmitted across networks — requires encryption to protect confidentiality.
concepts.ex: TLS 1.3 encrypts web traffic; VPN tunnels protect remote access.

concepts.tip: Data in use = in RAM/CPU. Hardest state to protect.
concepts.def: Data being actively processed in CPU or RAM — protected by memory encryption and access controls.
concepts.ex: Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) protect data during cloud processing.

concepts.def: Clearing is acceptable when media will be reused in the same physical environment for the same purposes

concepts.def: is the practice of searching through trash at homes and businesses to find valuable information

Media mgmt = track, protect, and safely dispose of storage media.
concepts.def: Controlling the lifecycle of storage media from procurement through secure disposal.
concepts.ex: Labeling tapes with classification, tracking chain of custody, degaussing before disposal.

concepts.tip: Labeling = stamps classification on media inside and out.
concepts.def: Marking physical and logical media with classification labels to guide proper handling.
concepts.ex: External tape label: 'SECRET — handle per policy X'; internal file metadata.

concepts.def: Inventory all mobile devices, including serial numbers, so they can be properly identified if they are stolen and then recovered.

concepts.def: Ensure workspaces are kept tidy so it is easy to tell when sensitive papers are left exposed, and routinely audit workspaces to ensure sensitive documents are not exposed.

concepts.def: Vaults Safes that are large enough to provide walk-in access

DLP = catch data sneaking out. Monitor, detect, block.
concepts.def: Tools and processes that detect and prevent unauthorized exfiltration of sensitive data.
concepts.ex: DLP blocks emailing SSNs; alerts when confidential files are copied to USB.

concepts.tip: DLP approach: identify → classify → monitor → enforce.
concepts.def: Identify sensitive data, classify it, monitor its movement, and enforce policy violations.
concepts.ex: Content inspection, fingerprinting, and tagging to track sensitive documents.

concepts.tip: Data protection strategy = layered: DLP + encryption + access control.
concepts.def: Comprehensive plan covering DLP, encryption, access control, and monitoring for data protection.
concepts.ex: Strategy layers encryption at rest, DLP at network, and CASB for cloud.

concepts.tip: DLP tuning = monitor first, tune, then block. Avoid false-positive chaos.
concepts.def: Deploy DLP in monitor-only mode, tune rules to reduce false positives, then switch to enforce.
concepts.ex: First week: log only; tune out false positives; week 3: block violations.

concepts.tip: NDLP = watches the wire. Catches data leaving the network.
concepts.def: Monitors network traffic for unauthorized transmission of sensitive data leaving the organization.
concepts.ex: NDLP appliance inspects email attachments and web uploads for credit card numbers.

concepts.def: Resiliency is the ability to deal with challenges, damage, and crises and bounce back to normal or near-normal condition in short order.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · General Approaches to DLP › Network DLP (NDLP)
EDLP = watches the device. Catches local data leakage.
concepts.def: Agent on endpoints monitoring file movement, USB use, print, and screen capture for policy violations.
concepts.ex: EDLP agent blocks copying confidential files to USB drive on laptop.

concepts.tip: 42010 = the standard defining what 'architecture description' means.
concepts.def: International standard defining fundamental concepts and vocabulary for architecture descriptions of systems.
concepts.ex: Defines architecture, view, viewpoint, stakeholder, and concern formally.

concepts.tip: Architecture = structure + relationships + principles of a system.
concepts.def: Fundamental organization of a system: its components, their relationships, and design principles.
concepts.ex: Three-tier web architecture: presentation, application, and data layers.

concepts.tip: AD = the document capturing the architecture via multiple views.
concepts.def: A work product expressing system architecture using one or more views and viewpoints.
concepts.ex: AD contains UML diagrams, deployment diagrams, and data flow diagrams.

concepts.tip: View = one angle on the system for one audience.
concepts.def: Representation of a system from the perspective of a specific set of stakeholders and concerns.
concepts.ex: Security view shows trust boundaries; operations view shows deployment topology.

concepts.tip: Viewpoint = the template/rules for building a view.
concepts.def: Specification of conventions for constructing, interpreting, and using a particular view.
concepts.ex: Security viewpoint defines notation, rules, and concerns for security views.

concepts.tip: Memory types: ROM=permanent, RAM=temporary, cache=fast buffer.
concepts.def: Categories of memory: ROM (non-volatile), RAM (volatile), cache, virtual — each with different speed and use.
concepts.ex: L1 cache fastest; RAM for running processes; ROM for BIOS/firmware.

concepts.tip: RAM = volatile. Power off = data gone. Fast but temporary.
concepts.def: Volatile primary storage holding active program instructions and data; lost when power is removed.
concepts.ex: Opening an app loads its code from disk into RAM for CPU execution.

concepts.tip: ROM = read only, non-volatile. Firmware lives here.
concepts.def: Non-volatile storage containing permanently written firmware or boot code.
concepts.ex: BIOS/UEFI firmware stored in ROM/flash; not erasable by normal software.

concepts.def: Level 1 (L1) is faster than Level 2 (L2), and L2 is faster than L3
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Memory Types
Memory mapping = give every resource an address the CPU can reach.
concepts.def: Assigning specific address ranges to RAM, ROM, and I/O devices in the CPU's address space.
concepts.ex: I/O-mapped vs. memory-mapped I/O — devices accessed like memory addresses.

concepts.tip: Buffer overflow = write past the edge, hijack execution. Use safe APIs.
concepts.def: Writing data beyond the end of an allocated buffer, overwriting adjacent memory and enabling code execution.
concepts.ex: strcpy() without bounds checking allows attacker to overwrite return address.

concepts.tip: Memory protection: ASLR (randomize) + DEP (no-execute) + canaries.
concepts.def: OS and hardware mechanisms preventing unauthorized memory access: ASLR, DEP, segmentation, paging.
concepts.ex: ASLR randomizes code locations; DEP marks data regions non-executable.

concepts.tip: Memory leak = allocate but never free. System slows then crashes.
concepts.def: Failure to release dynamically allocated memory, leading to gradual resource exhaustion and system instability.
concepts.ex: Loop allocates memory each iteration but never frees it — RAM exhausted after hours.

concepts.tip: Process mgmt = OS is the traffic cop for all running programs.
concepts.def: OS responsibility of creating, scheduling, running, and terminating processes.
concepts.ex: Windows Task Manager shows process states; OS scheduler allocates CPU time.

concepts.tip: Stack = LIFO. Call pushes, return pops. Overflow attacks the stack.
concepts.def: LIFO data structures used for function calls, return addresses, and local variable storage.
concepts.ex: Each function call pushes a stack frame; return pops it — overflow exploits this.

concepts.tip: Scheduling = OS decides who runs next and for how long.
concepts.def: OS algorithm determining which process gets CPU time and for how long.
concepts.ex: Round-robin, priority-based, shortest-job-first scheduling algorithms.

concepts.tip: Process states: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.
concepts.def: States a process moves through: new, ready, running, waiting/blocked, and terminated.
concepts.ex: Process moves: new → ready → running → waiting → ready → terminated.

concepts.tip: Process isolation = each process in its own sandbox. No peeking.
concepts.def: OS mechanism preventing one process from accessing or corrupting another process's memory.
concepts.ex: Virtual memory ensures process A cannot read process B's address space.

concepts.tip: Process > thread > task. Each is a different granularity of work.
concepts.def: OS terminology: process (running program), thread (execution unit within process), task (work unit).
concepts.ex: A browser process may have many threads for tabs and rendering.

concepts.tip: Memory mgmt = OS as banker: loans RAM, takes it back when done.
concepts.def: OS function of allocating, tracking, and reclaiming memory for processes through paging and swapping.
concepts.ex: OS uses page tables to map virtual addresses to physical RAM locations.

concepts.tip: Relocation = move a program anywhere in RAM and still run it.
concepts.def: OS ability to load a process into any available memory location and update address references.
concepts.ex: Compiler uses relative addresses; OS loader resolves them at load time.

concepts.tip: Protection = walls between processes and the kernel.
concepts.def: OS mechanisms preventing processes from interfering with each other's memory and kernel space.
concepts.ex: Memory protection unit (MPU) raises fault if process accesses forbidden address.

concepts.tip: Sharing = controlled access to common memory. IPC mechanism.
concepts.def: Controlled sharing of memory regions between processes for inter-process communication.
concepts.ex: Shared memory segment used between producer and consumer processes.

concepts.tip: Logical org = virtual address space the program sees.
concepts.def: How memory appears to programs: flat, segmented, or paged address spaces.
concepts.ex: Program sees 4GB flat virtual address space regardless of physical RAM size.

concepts.tip: Physical org = real hardware: chips, cache, DIMM slots.
concepts.def: Actual hardware memory layout: RAM chips, cache hierarchy, and physical addressing.
concepts.ex: L1/L2/L3 cache hierarchy sits between CPU registers and main RAM.

concepts.def: Every address reference is validated for protection.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Memory Management
Virtual memory = disk pretends to be RAM. Swap when RAM full.
concepts.def: Technique using disk space to extend available RAM, allowing more processes than physical memory.
concepts.ex: Windows pagefile.sys or Linux swap partition extends apparent RAM.

concepts.def: While this unencrypted data is sitting in RAM, the system could write out the data to the swap space on the hard drive in its unencrypted state
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Memory Management › Virtual Memory
I/O mgmt = OS as middleman between devices and programs.
concepts.def: OS control of I/O devices via device drivers, buffers, interrupt handlers, and DMA.
concepts.ex: Keyboard interrupt triggers OS to read key from I/O port and pass to app.

concepts.tip: I/O type: character (serial byte) vs. block (random access sectors).
concepts.def: I/O devices classified as character devices (sequential, byte-by-byte) or block devices (random access).
concepts.ex: Keyboard = character device; hard disk = block device.

concepts.tip: Interrupts = tap on CPU shoulder. Stop what you're doing, handle this.
concepts.def: Hardware or software signals causing CPU to pause current work and handle a priority event.
concepts.ex: Timer interrupt triggers OS scheduler; NIC interrupt announces incoming packet.

concepts.tip: DMA = device copies to RAM directly. CPU does other work meanwhile.
concepts.def: Direct Memory Access lets I/O controllers transfer data to RAM without CPU involvement.
concepts.ex: NIC uses DMA to write received packets directly to kernel buffers.

concepts.tip: CPU rings: ring 0 = kernel (all power), ring 3 = user (restricted).
concepts.def: How CPU design features (rings, privilege modes, caches) integrate with OS security mechanisms.
concepts.ex: x86 rings 0-3: kernel at ring 0, user apps at ring 3.

concepts.tip: Isolation = separation. Each entity in its own protected zone.
concepts.def: OS ensuring processes, users, and kernel are separated from each other to prevent interference.
concepts.ex: Hypervisor isolates VMs; OS isolates processes; kernel isolates from user space.

concepts.tip: CPU modes: user (restricted) vs. kernel (privileged). Syscall crosses boundary.
concepts.def: User mode (restricted, no direct hardware) and kernel/supervisor mode (full hardware access).
concepts.ex: System call switches from user mode to kernel mode to access hardware.

concepts.def: The higher the ring level that the process executes within, the larger the domain of resources that is available to it.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · CPU Architecture Integration
OS arch: monolithic (big) vs. microkernel (small + services).
concepts.def: Monolithic (one large kernel), microkernel (minimal kernel), layered, and exokernel designs.
concepts.ex: Linux = monolithic; Windows NT = hybrid microkernel; GNU Mach = microkernel.

concepts.tip: VM = OS inside OS. Hypervisor provides the illusion of hardware.
concepts.def: Software emulation of hardware allowing multiple isolated OS instances to run on one physical host.
concepts.ex: VMware ESXi runs Windows and Linux VMs simultaneously on one server.

concepts.tip: Security requirements = CIA translated into design constraints.
concepts.def: CIA-based requirements driving every security design decision in a system.
concepts.ex: 'Patient data must be encrypted at rest and in transit' — a CIA-derived requirement.

concepts.tip: Perimeter = the trust boundary. Inside = trusted; outside = not.
concepts.def: Logical boundary separating trusted internal components from untrusted external systems.
concepts.ex: Firewall marks the network perimeter; trusted computing base is the internal perimeter.

concepts.def: is an abstract machine that mediates all access subjects have to objects, both to ensure that the subjects have the necessary access rights and to protect the objects from unauthorized access and destructive modification.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Security Architecture Requirements

concepts.def: is made up of hardware, software, and firmware components that fall within the TCB, and it implements and enforces the reference monitor concept
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Security Architecture Requirements

concepts.def: it provides and addresses confidentiality only
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Security Models
BLP three rules: no read up, no write down, same-level RW.
concepts.def: Bell-LaPadula's three rules: simple security (no read up), *-property (no write down), strong star.
concepts.ex: Secret-cleared user: can read Confidential, can write Secret, cannot read TS.

concepts.tip: Simple security = no read up. Confidentiality rule.
concepts.def: Bell-LaPadula: a subject cannot read data at a higher classification than their clearance (no read up).
concepts.ex: Secret-cleared analyst cannot read Top Secret documents.

concepts.tip: Star property = no write down. Prevents leaking secrets downward.
concepts.def: Bell-LaPadula: a subject cannot write data to a lower classification level (no write down).
concepts.ex: Top Secret user cannot copy TS data into an Unclassified document.

concepts.tip: Strong star = read AND write only at your own level.
concepts.def: Bell-LaPadula: subjects can only read and write objects at their own classification level.
concepts.ex: Combines no-read-up and no-write-down — subjects stay at their level.

concepts.def: is a security model that addresses the integrity of data within a system
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Security Models
Biba *-integrity = no write up. Dirty data can't corrupt clean data.
concepts.def: Biba integrity model: a subject cannot write to an object at a higher integrity level (no write up).
concepts.ex: Low-trust process cannot modify high-integrity configuration files.

concepts.tip: Biba simple = no read down. High integrity ignores low-integrity data.
concepts.def: Biba integrity model: a subject cannot read from a lower integrity object (no read down).
concepts.ex: High-integrity process cannot read from low-integrity untrusted source.

concepts.tip: Invocation property = no calling up to higher integrity services.
concepts.def: Biba: a subject cannot request services from an object of higher integrity level.
concepts.ex: Low-trust application cannot invoke high-trust system service.

concepts.tip: Clark-Wilson = CDI + UDI + TP + IVP. Well-formed transactions only.
concepts.def: Integrity model using constrained data items (CDIs), unconstrained data items (UDIs), transformation procedures (TPs), and integrity verification procedures (IVPs).
concepts.ex: Accounting system: journal entries are CDIs; TPs are the only way to modify them.

concepts.tip: Noninterference = high actions invisible to low observers.
concepts.def: Security model ensuring actions at a higher security level don't affect what lower-level users can observe.
concepts.ex: TS operations must not change what Unclassified users can see or infer.

concepts.def: is a way for an entity to receive information in an unauthorized manner
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Noninterference Model

concepts.def: states that a subject can write to an object if, and only if, the subject cannot read another object that is in a different dataset.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Security Models
Graham-Denning = 8 rules. Create, delete, grant, revoke access rights.
concepts.def: Formal model defining 8 primitive commands for creating, deleting, and transferring access rights.
concepts.ex: Commands include: create object, create subject, grant access right, delete access right.

concepts.def: HRU model is used by software designers to ensure that no unforeseen vulnerability is introduced and the stated access control goals are achieved
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Security Models
Common Criteria = international security product evaluation standard.
concepts.def: International standard (ISO/IEC 15408) for evaluating and certifying the security of IT products.
concepts.ex: A firewall vendor gets CC EAL4+ certification for their product.

concepts.tip: EAL1–7: higher = more rigorous evaluation. EAL4 is commercial sweet spot.
concepts.def: CC assurance scale from EAL1 (functionally tested) to EAL7 (formally verified design and tested).
concepts.ex: EAL4 = methodically designed, tested, reviewed — common for commercial products.

concepts.tip: Security problem = threats + policies + assumptions for CC eval.
concepts.def: CC document defining threats, organizational security policies, and assumptions for the evaluation.
concepts.ex: Describes the threat agents, assets, and attack methods the TOE must counter.

concepts.tip: Security objectives = what the TOE must achieve to counter threats.
concepts.def: CC goals countering the defined threats and satisfying security policies for the TOE and environment.
concepts.ex: Objective: TOE must authenticate users before granting access to resources.

concepts.def: These are very specific requirements for compliant products. They are detailed enough for implementation by system developers, and for evaluation by independent laboratories.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Common Criteria（CC) › protection profile
CC components = SFR + SAR building blocks. Assembled into PPs.
concepts.def: CC building blocks: functional and assurance components organized into packages and profiles.
concepts.ex: FIA_UAU.2 = user authentication before action — a CC functional component.

concepts.tip: PP = generic security wishlist for a product type. No specific product.
concepts.def: Implementation-independent statement of security requirements for a category of IT product.
concepts.ex: US Government PP for General Purpose OS defines requirements for Windows/Linux evaluation.

concepts.tip: TOE = the exact product under evaluation. Specific version.
concepts.def: The specific IT product or system being evaluated under Common Criteria.
concepts.ex: A specific version of a firewall product is the TOE for CC evaluation.

concepts.tip: Security target = vendor's specific security claim for their TOE.
concepts.def: Implementation-specific CC document claiming security properties for a specific TOE.
concepts.ex: Vendor writes ST claiming their firewall meets EAL4 assurance for their specific product.

concepts.tip: SFR = what the TOE must DO. Functional behavior requirements.
concepts.def: CC requirements specifying desired security behavior of the TOE (authentication, audit, crypto, etc.).
concepts.ex: SFR FPT_STM.1 — TOE must provide reliable time stamps.

concepts.tip: SAR = how we VERIFY the TOE does what it claims.
concepts.def: CC requirements specifying how confidence in the TOE's correct security implementation is established.
concepts.ex: SAR ALC_DVS.1 — developer must have security measures for the development environment.

concepts.def: Functional and assurance requirements are bundled into packages for reuse.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Common Criteria（CC) › Components

concepts.def: is the comprehensive technical evaluation of the security components and their compliance for the purpose of accreditation.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Certification vs. Accreditation

concepts.def: is the formal acceptance of the adequacy of a system’s overall security and functionality by management
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Certification vs. Accreditation
C&A: certify the tech, accredit (authorize) the operation.
concepts.def: C&A process: certification verifies technical security; accreditation authorizes system to operate.
concepts.ex: US federal systems undergo C&A (now NIST RMF) before going live.

concepts.def: Systems described as open are built upon standards, protocols, and interfaces that have published specifications.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Open vs. Closed Systems
Closed = vendor lock-in. No standard interfaces.
concepts.def: Proprietary systems with vendor-controlled hardware and software, limiting interoperability.
concepts.ex: IBM mainframes, Apple ecosystem — integration requires vendor cooperation.

concepts.tip: Cloud = IaaS (infra), PaaS (platform), SaaS (software) on demand.
concepts.def: On-demand delivery of computing resources (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) over the internet with pay-per-use pricing.
concepts.ex: AWS EC2 (IaaS), Google App Engine (PaaS), Salesforce (SaaS).

concepts.tip: Parallel = divide and conquer simultaneously. Many processors, one task.
concepts.def: Simultaneous execution using multiple processors or cores to solve computationally intensive problems faster.
concepts.ex: GPU clusters for machine learning; MapReduce for big data processing.

concepts.tip: Bit parallelism = wider data bus = more bits per clock cycle.
concepts.def: Processing multiple bits simultaneously by using wider data paths (32-bit vs. 64-bit processors).
concepts.ex: 64-bit CPU processes data twice as wide per cycle as 32-bit.

concepts.tip: Databases: ACID + SQL + access control. Watch for SQL injection.
concepts.def: Structured data stores with ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) and query languages.
concepts.ex: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL — support roles, views, and encryption.

concepts.def: is the act of combining information from separate sources
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Database Systems

concepts.def: is the ability to derive information not explicitly available.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Database Systems

concepts.def: is a technique used to hide specific cells that contain information that could be used in inference attacks
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Database Systems › Inference

concepts.def: is a technique of inserting bogus information in the hopes of misdirecting an attacker or confusing the matter enough that the actual attack will not be fruitful.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Database Systems › Inference
Web systems = OWASP Top 10. XSS, SQLi, CSRF are the top threats.
concepts.def: Applications delivered through web browsers — vulnerable to XSS, SQL injection, CSRF, and clickjacking.
concepts.ex: OWASP Top 10 addresses the most critical web application security risks.

concepts.tip: Mobile risks: lost device + rogue app + public Wi-Fi.
concepts.def: Smartphones and tablets with unique risks: device theft, rogue apps, insecure Wi-Fi, and mobile malware.
concepts.ex: MDM solutions enforce PIN, encryption, and remote wipe on corporate devices.

concepts.tip: CPS = software controls physical world. Safety + security critical.
concepts.def: Integration of computation with physical processes in systems like autonomous vehicles and medical devices.
concepts.ex: Insulin pump controlled by embedded software — compromise could harm patient.

concepts.tip: IoT = many tiny connected devices, mostly without security by design.
concepts.def: Network of embedded devices with sensors connecting to the internet — often with minimal security controls.
concepts.ex: Smart thermostats, cameras, industrial sensors — frequently unpatched and insecure.

concepts.tip: ICS = software running critical infrastructure. Stuxnet targeted ICS.
concepts.def: Computer systems controlling physical industrial processes including SCADA, DCS, and PLCs.
concepts.ex: Power plant control systems, oil pipeline SCADA, factory PLCs.

concepts.tip: SCADA = remote industrial control. Distributed and critical.
concepts.def: ICS for real-time monitoring and control of geographically distributed infrastructure.
concepts.ex: Water treatment plant SCADA monitoring chemical levels across multiple sites.

concepts.tip: ICS security: segment OT from IT, air gap critical systems.
concepts.def: Securing OT environments: air gaps, network segmentation, patching challenges, and safety-first design.
concepts.ex: Segmenting ICS networks from corporate IT; strict change management for patches.

concepts.def: Ensure there is a process for patch management.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Industrial Control Systems(ICS) › ICS Security
Maintenance hook = developer's secret backdoor. Remove before production!
concepts.def: Undocumented backdoors left by developers for maintenance access — a significant security vulnerability.
concepts.ex: Hard-coded maintenance account in firmware allowing remote access without authentication.

concepts.def: Stegomedium The medium in which the information is hidden

concepts.def: Provides confidentiality but not authenticity or nonrepudiation.

concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Types of Symmetric Systems

concepts.def: Errors are contained. If an error takes place during the encryption process, it only affects one block of data.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Data Encryption Standard (DES) › DES Modes

concepts.def: provides: digital signatures, secure key distribution, and encryption.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Types of Asymmetric Systems

concepts.def: provides: digital signatures, secure key distribution, and encryption.

concepts.def: was discovered to be insecure and is not currently used in cryptosystems
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Types of Asymmetric Systems

concepts.def: A message can be encrypted, which provides confidentiality.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Applying Cryptography

concepts.term: Rules for Keys and Key Management
concepts.def: Keys should be stored and transmitted by secure means.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Key Management › Key Management Principles

concepts.def: Brownout Prolonged power supply that is below normal voltage
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Electric Power Issues › different types of voltage fluctuations

concepts.def: can be configured to sound an alarm either when a predefined temperature (fixed temperature) is reached or when the temperature increases over time (rate-of-rise)
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression › Types of Fire Detection

concepts.def: The most effective replacement for halon is FM-200
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Environmental Issues › Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression

concepts.def: A thermal-fusible link on the sprinkler head has to melt before the water is released.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression › Water Sprinklers

concepts.def: A network protocol is a standard set of rules that determines how systems will communicate across networks.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Open Systems Interconnection Reference Model
Layer 7 = Application. HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS live here.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 7 — provides network services directly to user applications (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS).
concepts.ex: Web browser uses HTTP at Layer 7; email client uses SMTP.

concepts.tip: Layer 6 = Presentation. Format, encrypt, compress data.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 6 — handles data formatting, encryption, compression, and character encoding.
concepts.ex: SSL/TLS in the OSI model sits at Layer 6; JPEG compression.

concepts.tip: Layer 5 = Session. Start, manage, end conversations.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 5 — establishes, manages, and terminates communication sessions between applications.
concepts.ex: NetBIOS, RPC, and SQL session management operate at Layer 5.

concepts.tip: Layer 4 = Transport. TCP (reliable) vs. UDP (fast). Ports here.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 4 — provides end-to-end communication, segmentation, and error recovery (TCP/UDP).
concepts.ex: TCP at Layer 4 ensures reliable delivery; UDP provides fast, unreliable delivery.

concepts.tip: Layer 3 = Network. IP addresses and routing. Routers live here.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 3 — routes packets between networks using logical IP addresses.
concepts.ex: Routers operate at Layer 3; IP addressing and packet forwarding.

concepts.tip: Layer 2 = Data Link. MAC addresses and frames. Switches here.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 2 — provides MAC addressing, framing, and error detection within a network segment.
concepts.ex: Ethernet frames (MAC addresses), switches operate at Layer 2.

concepts.tip: Layer 1 = Physical. Bits on the wire, cable, or radio.
concepts.def: OSI Layer 1 — transmits raw bits over physical medium (cables, radio waves, fiber).
concepts.ex: Cat6 cables, fiber optics, radio signals — all Layer 1.

concepts.tip: Multilayer = protocols crossing OSI layer boundaries.
concepts.def: Protocols that span or operate across multiple OSI layers simultaneously.
concepts.ex: IPsec operates at Layer 3 but also affects Layers 4-7; SSL/TLS spans Layers 4-7.

concepts.def: is a communications protocol designed for use in SCADA systems, particularly those within the power sector
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Multilayer Protocols

concepts.def: Another multilayer protocol that had almost no security features until very recently is the one that runs most automobiles worldwide.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Multilayer Protocols
TCP = reliable, ordered, connection-oriented. SYN-SYN/ACK-ACK.
concepts.def: Transmission Control Protocol — reliable, connection-oriented protocol with ordered delivery and error correction.
concepts.ex: TCP three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK before data transfer.

concepts.tip: Ports: 0–1023 well-known, 1024–49151 registered, rest ephemeral.
concepts.def: Well-known ports (0–1023), registered (1024–49151), dynamic/private (49152–65535).
concepts.ex: HTTP=80, HTTPS=443 (well-known); MySQL=3306 (registered).

concepts.tip: IP = logical address for routing. IPv4=32bit, IPv6=128bit.
concepts.def: Logical addresses identifying network interfaces: IPv4 (32-bit) and IPv6 (128-bit).

concepts.tip: IPv6 = 128 bits, IPsec native, auto-config. Replaces IPv4.
concepts.def: 128-bit IP addressing replacing IPv4 with larger address space, built-in IPsec, and auto-configuration.
concepts.ex: 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334 — 128 bits in hex notation.

concepts.tip: Auto tunneling = wrap IPv6 in IPv4 to cross old networks.
concepts.def: Encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 headers for transit across IPv4-only networks.
concepts.ex: 6in4, 6to4, Teredo — all tunnel IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

concepts.tip: 6to4 = embeds IPv4 in IPv6 2002::/16 prefix.
concepts.def: Embeds IPv4 address in IPv6 prefix (2002::/16) to tunnel IPv6 traffic over IPv4 internet.

concepts.tip: Teredo = IPv6 through NAT via UDP 3544.
concepts.def: Microsoft IPv6 tunneling protocol enabling NAT traversal using UDP port 3544.
concepts.ex: Windows uses Teredo to connect IPv6 hosts behind IPv4 NAT.

concepts.def: is used for connectivity of systems within a specific network
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · IPv6 › Automatic tunneling
Layer 2 security: MACsec (802.1AE) encrypts frames, 802.1AR authenticates.
concepts.def: IEEE standards (802.1AE MACsec, 802.1AR DevID) securing data link layer communications.
concepts.ex: MACsec encrypts Ethernet frames hop-by-hop between network devices.

concepts.tip: 802.1AR = hardware device identity certificate. Birth certificate for devices.
concepts.def: Standard for secure device identity using manufacturer-issued device identifiers (IDevID/LDevID).
concepts.ex: 802.1AR certificate embedded in switch hardware at manufacturing time.

concepts.tip: Converged = storage + data on one IP network. Simplifies cabling.
concepts.def: Combining multiple network functions or protocols into a single IP infrastructure.
concepts.ex: FCoE and iSCSI converge storage traffic onto standard Ethernet networks.

concepts.tip: FCoE = storage over Ethernet. Merges FC and Ethernet networks.
concepts.def: Protocol encapsulating Fibre Channel storage frames over standard Ethernet networks.
concepts.ex: Data center replaces separate FC SAN and Ethernet with one FCoE network.

concepts.def: MPLS is considered a converged protocol because it can encapsulate any higher-layer protocol and tunnel it over a variety of links.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Converged Protocols
iSCSI = SCSI over IP. Block storage over TCP/IP network.
concepts.def: Block-level storage protocol encapsulating SCSI commands over standard TCP/IP networks.
concepts.ex: Server accesses SAN disk over iSCSI using regular Ethernet instead of Fibre Channel.

concepts.tip: IP convergence = one network for everything. Voice + video + data.
concepts.def: Using IP infrastructure to carry voice, video, storage, and data on a single unified network.
concepts.ex: VoIP phones, video conferencing, and data all sharing same IP network.

concepts.tip: Transmission types: simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex. Also analog vs. digital.
concepts.def: Analog vs. digital; simplex (one-way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (simultaneous both ways).
concepts.ex: Walkie-talkie = half-duplex; phone call = full-duplex.

concepts.tip: Digital = binary 0/1. Cleaner signal, more noise-resistant than analog.
concepts.def: Discrete binary (0/1) signal representation — more noise-resistant than analog.
concepts.ex: Ethernet uses digital signaling; more reliable over long distances.

concepts.def: Data throughput values can be higher than bandwidth values if compression mechanisms are implemented.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · signal › Digital
Async = no shared clock. Start/stop bits wrap each byte.
concepts.def: Data transmission without a shared clock — start/stop bits frame each character.
concepts.ex: Serial COM port (RS-232) uses asynchronous transmission.

concepts.tip: Sync = shared clock. Faster for bulk data, no start/stop overhead.
concepts.def: Data transmission with a shared clock signal enabling higher efficiency for bulk data.
concepts.ex: T1 lines, synchronous serial — clock signal keeps sender and receiver in sync.

concepts.tip: Baseband = whole pipe for one signal. Ethernet uses baseband.
concepts.def: Single digital signal using the entire bandwidth — one transmission at a time (Ethernet).
concepts.ex: Ethernet (10Base-T, 100Base-TX) uses baseband signaling.

concepts.tip: Broadband = multiple signals, frequency divided. Cable TV model.
concepts.def: Multiple signals sharing bandwidth via frequency division — supports simultaneous channels.
concepts.ex: Cable TV and internet coexist on same coax using different frequency bands.

concepts.tip: Cabling: twisted-pair (cheap), coax (TV), fiber (fast, long).
concepts.def: Physical wire transmission media — twisted-pair, coaxial, and fiber-optic cables.
concepts.ex: Cat6 twisted-pair for LAN; multimode fiber for backbone; coax for cable TV.

concepts.tip: Twisted-pair = copper, cheap, EMI-resistant. Cat5e/Cat6 for LAN.
concepts.def: Copper wire pairs twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference — used in Ethernet and telephony.
concepts.ex: Cat5e supports 1 Gbps; Cat6 supports 10 Gbps at shorter distances.

concepts.tip: Fiber = light, not electricity. Fast, EMI-immune, long distance.
concepts.def: Transmits data as light pulses — immune to EMI, high bandwidth, and suitable for long distances.
concepts.ex: Single-mode fiber spans kilometers; multimode for building backbone.

concepts.tip: Fiber components: core + cladding + transmitter + receiver.
concepts.def: Core (light path), cladding (reflection), buffer, jacket, plus transmitters, receivers, and connectors.
concepts.ex: SC, LC, ST connectors; laser or LED transmitters; photodiode receivers.

concepts.tip: Fiber light: LED for short (multimode), laser for long (single-mode).
concepts.def: Fiber optics use LED (multimode) or laser diodes (single-mode) to generate light signals.
concepts.ex: Laser diodes for long-haul single-mode; LEDs for short multimode links.

concepts.tip: Single-mode = laser, long distance. Multimode = LED, short runs.
concepts.def: Glass or plastic core that transmits light — single-mode (long, narrow) or multimode (short, wide).
concepts.ex: Single-mode: 9µm core, kilometers. Multimode: 50/62.5µm core, hundreds of meters.

concepts.tip: Cable problems: EMI, crosstalk, attenuation. Fiber avoids most.
concepts.def: EMI, crosstalk, attenuation, impedance mismatch — all degrade cable signal quality.
concepts.ex: Crosstalk between parallel cables; attenuation limits maximum cable length.

concepts.tip: Wireless methods: RF (Wi-Fi/cellular), IR (remotes), microwave (satellites).
concepts.def: Methods for transmitting data wirelessly: RF, infrared, microwave, each with range and security tradeoffs.
concepts.ex: Wi-Fi uses RF; TV remotes use IR; cellular uses microwave RF.

concepts.tip: Spread spectrum: FHSS (hops) + DSSS (spreads). Hard to jam or intercept.
concepts.def: Spreads signal across a wide frequency band to resist jamming, interception, and interference.
concepts.ex: FHSS hops frequencies; DSSS spreads signal across band — both used in 802.11.

concepts.tip: OFDM = many parallel sub-carriers. Modern Wi-Fi and LTE use it.
concepts.def: Multi-carrier modulation dividing channel into sub-carriers to improve spectral efficiency and resist multipath.
concepts.ex: OFDM used in 802.11a/g/n/ac/ax, LTE, and cable modems.

concepts.tip: WLAN components: AP + NIC + antenna + controller + RADIUS.
concepts.def: Access points (APs), wireless NICs, antennas, WLAN controllers, and authentication servers.
concepts.ex: AP broadcasts SSID; clients associate; RADIUS server authenticates.

concepts.tip: WLAN security: WEP broken → WPA flawed → WPA2 AES → WPA3 SAE.
concepts.def: WEP (broken) → WPA (TKIP, flawed) → WPA2 (AES-CCMP) → WPA3 (SAE, enhanced).
concepts.ex: WEP cracked in minutes; WPA2 enterprise with 802.1X is the current minimum.

concepts.tip: 802.11 original = 2 Mbps, 2.4 GHz. The ancestor of all Wi-Fi.
concepts.def: Original 1997 Wi-Fi standard operating at 2.4 GHz, providing up to 2 Mbps using DSSS or FHSS.
concepts.ex: Legacy 802.11 — obsolete, superseded by 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ax.

concepts.def: WEP is considered insecure and should not be used.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Evolution of WLAN Security › IEEE Standard 802.11
802.11i = RSN security standard. AES-CCMP replaces WEP.
concepts.def: Security amendment to 802.11 defining Robust Security Network (RSN) using AES-CCMP.
concepts.ex: 802.11i replaced WEP with CCMP/AES and defined 4-way handshake.

concepts.term: IEEE 802.11i or Wi-Fi Protected Access II (WPA2)
concepts.tip: WPA2 = AES-CCMP + 802.1X (enterprise) or PSK (personal).
concepts.def: Enterprise and personal Wi-Fi security using AES-CCMP encryption and 802.1X authentication.
concepts.ex: WPA2-Enterprise with RADIUS; WPA2-Personal with pre-shared key (PSK).

concepts.tip: 802.1X = authenticate before connecting. Port blocks until approved.
concepts.def: Port-based network access control standard requiring authentication before granting LAN or WLAN access.
concepts.ex: Switch port blocks all traffic until user authenticates via RADIUS server.

concepts.tip: 802.1X = needs RADIUS + EAP. Three-party auth: supplicant-AP-RADIUS.
concepts.def: 802.1X requires a backend RADIUS server and EAP to perform enterprise authentication.
concepts.ex: Without RADIUS, 802.1X cannot function in enterprise mode.

concepts.tip: LEAP = Cisco old EAP, broken. Use PEAP or EAP-TLS instead.
concepts.def: Cisco proprietary EAP variant using MS-CHAPv2 — deprecated due to dictionary attack vulnerabilities.
concepts.ex: LEAP replaced by PEAP or EAP-TLS in modern Cisco deployments.

concepts.tip: PEAP = TLS tunnel wraps inner auth. Protects credentials in transit.
concepts.def: EAP variant creating an encrypted TLS tunnel protecting inner authentication credentials.
concepts.ex: PEAP-MSCHAPv2 is widely used for enterprise Wi-Fi authentication.

concepts.def: EAP-TTLS is designed to provide authentication that is as strong as EAP-TLS
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Evolution of WLAN Security › IEEE Standard 802.1X
Wi-Fi generations: b/g (2.4), a/ac (5), n/ax (dual-band).
concepts.def: 802.11 family defining Wi-Fi speeds and frequencies: a(5GHz), b(2.4GHz), g, n, ac, ax (Wi-Fi 6).
concepts.ex: 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) supports OFDMA and targets dense environments.

concepts.tip: Bluetooth = 10m, 2.4 GHz, PAN. Bluejacking/Bluesnarfing are threats.
concepts.def: Short-range (10m) personal area network using 2.4 GHz — risks include bluejacking, bluesnarfing, eavesdropping.
concepts.ex: Bluetooth headset, keyboard, IoT device pairing — secure pairing is critical.

concepts.def: If you must support unauthenticated users (e.g., visitors), ensure they are connected to an untrusted VLAN that remains outside your network’s perimeter.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Wireless Networks
Satellites: GEO (high latency), MEO (GPS), LEO (low latency).
concepts.def: Geostationary (35,786 km), MEO, and LEO satellites for global communications with latency and jamming risks.
concepts.ex: GEO for TV broadcast; LEO (Starlink) for low-latency internet.

concepts.tip: Mobile = cellular. 2G→3G→4G(LTE)→5G. Security improved each gen.
concepts.def: Cellular networks providing mobile connectivity — 2G/3G/4G LTE/5G generations.
concepts.ex: 4G LTE provides 100 Mbps+; 5G targets sub-millisecond latency.

concepts.tip: Multiple access: TDMA (time), FDMA (frequency), CDMA (code), OFDMA.
concepts.def: TDMA, FDMA, CDMA, and OFDMA techniques sharing radio spectrum among multiple simultaneous users.
concepts.ex: GSM uses TDMA; CDMA2000 uses CDMA; LTE uses OFDMA.

concepts.tip: Mobile gens: 1G analog, 2G digital, 3G data, 4G LTE, 5G NR.
concepts.def: 1G (analog voice), 2G (digital voice/SMS), 3G (mobile data), 4G (LTE broadband), 5G (ultra-low latency).
concepts.ex: 2G = GSM; 3G = UMTS/HSPA; 4G = LTE; 5G = NR.

concepts.tip: Topology = shape of the network. Star most common; mesh most resilient.
concepts.def: Physical or logical arrangement of network nodes — bus, ring, star, mesh, and hybrid topologies.
concepts.ex: Star topology: all devices connect to central switch. Most common LAN topology.

concepts.tip: Media access = who can talk when. CSMA/CD for Ethernet.
concepts.def: Methods controlling how devices share a common transmission medium — CSMA, token passing.
concepts.ex: Ethernet uses CSMA/CD; Token Ring uses token passing.

concepts.def: A token is a 24-bit control frame used to control which computers communicate at what intervals.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Media Access Technologies
CSMA = listen before transmit. 'Sense' the carrier first.
concepts.def: Carrier Sense Multiple Access — devices listen for carrier signal before transmitting to avoid collisions.
concepts.ex: Device checks if medium is idle before sending; if busy, waits.

concepts.tip: CSMA/CD = wired Ethernet. Detect collision, back off, retry.
concepts.def: CSMA with Collision Detection — used in wired Ethernet; detects collisions and retransmits after random backoff.
concepts.ex: IEEE 802.3 Ethernet uses CSMA/CD for half-duplex operation.

concepts.tip: CSMA/CA = wireless Wi-Fi. Avoid collision before it happens.
concepts.def: CSMA with Collision Avoidance — used in 802.11 Wi-Fi; avoids collisions before they happen.
concepts.ex: 802.11 stations use RTS/CTS to reserve medium before transmitting.

concepts.def: is a method of monitoring multiple devices and controlling network access transmission
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Media Access Technologies
Ethernet = 802.3, wired LAN. CSMA/CD, MAC addresses, frames.
concepts.def: IEEE 802.3 standard for wired LAN — most widely deployed networking technology.
concepts.ex: 10/100/1000 Mbps Ethernet over twisted-pair Cat5e/Cat6 cables.

concepts.tip: 100Base-TX = 100 Mbps, Cat5, twisted-pair. Fast Ethernet.
concepts.def: Fast Ethernet standard: 100 Mbps over Cat5 twisted-pair cable using two pairs.
concepts.ex: 100Base-TX replaced 10Base-T in 1990s corporate LANs.

concepts.tip: 1000Base-T = 1 Gbps, Cat5e/Cat6, 4-pair. Standard gigabit LAN.
concepts.def: Gigabit Ethernet over Cat5e/Cat6 twisted-pair at 1 Gbps using all four pairs.
concepts.ex: 1000Base-T is the standard for modern desktop and server Ethernet connections.

concepts.def: is a LAN media access technology that enables the communication and sharing of networking resources.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Media Access Technologies
FDDI = 100 Mbps, fiber, dual ring. 1990s backbone tech.
concepts.def: Fiber Distributed Data Interface — 100 Mbps dual counter-rotating ring LAN using fiber optic.
concepts.ex: FDDI used as campus backbone in the 1990s; ring redundancy for fault tolerance.

concepts.tip: Unicast=one, Multicast=group, Broadcast=everyone.
concepts.def: Unicast (one-to-one), multicast (one-to-many), and broadcast (one-to-all) data delivery.
concepts.ex: Video stream = unicast; IPTV = multicast; ARP request = broadcast.

concepts.def: was created after RARP to enhance the functionality that RARP provides for diskless workstations
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Network Protocols and Services
ICMP = ping and traceroute. Diagnostic and error messages.
concepts.def: Network layer protocol for diagnostics (ping, traceroute) and error reporting between IP devices.
concepts.ex: Ping uses ICMP echo request/reply; traceroute uses ICMP TTL exceeded.

concepts.tip: SNMP = monitor and manage network devices. MIB + OID + community string.
concepts.def: Protocol for monitoring and managing network devices using managers, agents, and MIBs.
concepts.ex: SNMP manager polls router CPU utilization via SNMP GET request.

concepts.tip: SNMPv3 = finally secure. AuthNoPriv or AuthPriv with encryption.
concepts.def: SNMP version 3 adds authentication (MD5/SHA) and encryption (DES/AES) to address SNMPv1/v2 weaknesses.
concepts.ex: SNMPv3 authPriv mode: both authenticated and encrypted SNMP traffic.

concepts.tip: DNS = phone book of the internet. Name → IP address.
concepts.def: Distributed hierarchical system translating human-readable domain names to IP addresses.
concepts.ex: Browser queries DNS resolver to resolve www.example.com to 93.184.216.34.

concepts.tip: DNS threats: cache poison, spoofing, amplification DDoS. Use DNSSEC.
concepts.def: DNS cache poisoning, spoofing, DDoS amplification, and NXDOMAIN attacks targeting DNS infrastructure.
concepts.ex: Cache poisoning redirects users to attacker-controlled IP for legitimate domain.

concepts.tip: Email: SMTP sends, IMAP/POP3 receive. Always use TLS encryption.
concepts.def: SMTP for sending email; IMAP and POP3 for retrieval — require encryption (STARTTLS/SSL) and authentication.
concepts.ex: SMTP over port 587 (STARTTLS) for submission; IMAPS port 993.

concepts.tip: POP = downloads and removes email from server. One-device model.
concepts.def: Protocol for retrieving email from server — typically downloads and deletes messages from server.
concepts.ex: POP3 on port 110 (or 995 for SSL) downloads mail to local client.

concepts.tip: Email relay = SMTP forwards mail. Open relay = spammer magnet.
concepts.def: SMTP servers forwarding email on behalf of others — open relays exploited for spam campaigns.
concepts.ex: Misconfigured SMTP server accepts relay from any host — spammers exploit it.

concepts.def: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol(IS-IS)
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Routing Protocols

concepts.def: A Private Branch Exchange (PBX) is a private telephone switch that is located on a company’s property
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Network Components

concepts.def: Each protocol that is to be monitored must have a unique proxy.
concepts.tip: Mind map CISSP · Proxy › Application-level proxies
